reading.body:
Carrie Adams is named on three AI lobbying filings, all filed through one firm for a single client, and those filings name fifteen separate bills.

The concentration is the story. Three filings, one firm, one client, fifteen bills. A single registered lobbyist is the disclosed point of contact between one AI policy organization and a legislative agenda that spans both chambers and both parties' bill numbering. The prior government positions listed, Communications Director and Senior Advisor for one senator, Deputy Digital Director for another, Digital Director for a Speaker, and staff roles on the House Rules Committee and for two representatives, are disclosed because the Lobbying Disclosure Act requires covered positions from the prior twenty years. That is a staffing fact, not an inference about influence.

For AI specifically, this is the visible layer of the policy process that runs alongside the compute buildout. Data centers, interconnection queues, and power contracts are settled by regulators and utilities, but the statutory rules that shape what AI companies may do, what they must disclose, and how they are taxed move through bills like the fifteen listed here. Lobbying filings are one of the few places that process leaves a public trace.

What this does not show: the substance of any bill, whether any bill advanced, how much was spent, or what was communicated. It does not show that the prior government roles and the current client are connected, only that both are disclosed on the same filing. It covers one lobbyist, one firm, and one client, and says nothing about the rest of the field.
